source.title: Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity
source.authors: Scott Pesme; Loucas Pillaud-Vivien; Nicolas Flammarion

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether stochasticity changes generalization for diagonal linear networks, using stochastic gradient flow and sparse-regression validation loss rather than the claim versions' natural-label classification settings.
record.gate_note: The reported sparse-regression experiments compare SGD, gradient descent, and stochastic-gradient-flow trajectories and validation losses. Theoretical results about implicit bias and convergence are stated, but rows capture the experimental outcomes that bear on the catalog claim. Cited findings are not recorded as rows. Figure-only comparisons have no exact values stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study tests stochastic versus full-batch gradient methods in diagonal linear sparse regression, which matches none of V1–V8. In particular, V4 requires an adaptive-optimizer comparison; neither GD nor SGF is adaptive. The SGD–GD comparison also does not test V5's fixed-epoch batch-size effect on image classifiers or language models.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors prove, under stated step-size and probability conditions, that their stochastic gradient flow converges to an interpolator minimizing hyperbolic entropy at a smaller effective initialization than gradient flow. They interpret this as a stronger sparsity-inducing bias, controlled by the integrated training loss, and experimentally show better SGD prediction performance on synthetic sparse regression. The formal theorem characterizes implicit bias rather than proving a universal ordering of population prediction losses.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies diagonal linear networks on overparameterized noiseless sparse regression and models SGD with stochastic gradient flow; it does not test the natural-label classification settings in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale α changes the validation-loss comparison; the loss integral and convergence speed govern the stochastic bias. Injected label noise further slows training-loss convergence and changes validation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched initialization and step size, SGD achieves lower population prediction loss than GD in synthetic sparse regression with diagonal linear networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochasticity can improve the implicit bias and population prediction performance of diagonal linear networks on sparse regression.

fits_no_version.finding: GD initialized at the effective scale computed from an SGD trajectory approximately recovers SGD's solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD's implicit bias can approximately correspond to GD's bias from a smaller, trajectory-dependent initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD and the proposed stochastic gradient flow have similar training- and validation-loss trajectories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed stochastic gradient flow approximates SGD's dynamics in the tested sparse-regression setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Transient label-noise injection improves prediction loss relative to ordinary SGD at t = 10^6, while slowing training convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured label noise can strengthen sparsity-inducing implicit bias and improve prediction in diagonal linear sparse regression.

record.problems: Experiments use a small synthetic sparse-regression setup (n = 40, d = 100). Several plotted comparisons have no exact numerical values in the text. The stochastic-gradient-flow noise model approximates SGD noise; the authors describe experimental validation of that model. The injected-label-noise run had not converged at the reported evaluation point.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible numeric results beyond the five extracted rows. Figure-only exact values were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Coexistence of fixed-random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level held-out performance with random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD, tuning dependence, weight decay, and optimizer switching.

Large-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets on image or language workloads, and recipes that remove the penalty. Appendix A's effective-step-size formulas do not establish this performance comparison.
Dropout's effects on held-out error and its dependence on training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance as a predictor of generalization gaps and comparison with other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 links and limits_scope verdicts should be removed. A different task setting alone is not evidence that a version needs qualification when its defining optimizer comparison is absent. States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; the reported sparse-regression effects themselves are supported by the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization alongside natural-label generalization is not tested.
No width sweep or test-error comparison across widths is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison is reported.
Tests SGD versus GD only on a diagonal linear network in sparse regression; no adaptive optimizer, classification, language task, or broader hyperparameter tuning comparison.
No sharpness, perturbation tolerance, or competing generalization-measure comparison is reported.
No memorized-example removal or retraining experiment is reported.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained on sparse regression with Gaussian features; compared with GD at the same initialization scale and step size.
rows.measure: Validation loss at convergence or across the plotted trajectory
rows.baseline: GD validation loss; exact value not stated
rows.value: SGD converges towards a solution which generalises better than GD; exact value figure only
rows.note: The text describes the comparison but gives no exact validation-loss values.
rows.check: The reported SGD advantage over GD is supported, but no adaptive optimizer is tested, so this cannot establish V4. SGD is an algorithm, not a model.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD with GD and SGD-initialization-matched GD; the latter was initialized at the effective scale computed from the SGD trajectory.
rows.measure: Test loss of the recovered solution
rows.baseline: GD initialized at α; exact value not stated
rows.value: SGD generalises better than GD initialized at α; exact value figure only
rows.note: The paper calls this test loss, while Section 5.1 describes the same norm as validation loss under the stated population covariance.
rows.check: The SGD advantage at α = 0.01 is supported but bears on no listed version. Comparing SGD with GD does not test adaptive versus nonadaptive optimization.

rows.subject: GD initialized at α∞
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent initialized at the effective initialization scale computed from a prior SGD run.

conditions.value: α = 0.01 for initial SGD run; α∞ computed from that trajectory

rows.measure: Test loss of the recovered solution
rows.baseline: SGD initialized at α; exact value not stated
rows.value: GD from α∞ converges to approximately the same point as SGD from α; exact value figure only
rows.note: The authors state the correspondence is approximate for SGD and GD; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: Matching GD's initialization to an effective scale computed from SGD tests the proposed implicit-bias mechanism, not V4. The text supports approximate correspondence of the recovered solutions.

rows.subject: SGD and stochastic gradient flow (SGF)
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD and Euler-discretized SGF trajectories against GD.
rows.baseline: GD trajectory; exact values not stated
rows.value: SGD and SGF validation-loss trajectories have very similar behaviours; exact values figure only
rows.note: This validates the continuous model, but does not state that SGD beats GD in this comparison.
rows.check: This is validation of the study's SGF approximation against SGD. The relevant comparator is SGD versus SGF, rather than GD as recorded. Similar trajectories do not constitute partial evidence for V4.

rows.subject: SGD with injected label noise
rows.operation_detail: Injected label noise with δt = 1 for t ≤ 10³ and δt = 0 thereafter.

conditions.value: Δt ∼ unif{2δt, −2δt}; δt = 1 if t ≤ 10³, then 0

rows.measure: Validation loss of the recovered solution
rows.baseline: SGD without injected label noise; exact value not stated
rows.value: The solution with injected label noise is much better than that of SGD; it has not even converged yet; exact value figure only
rows.note: The result compares a modified SGD recipe and reports the noisy run had not converged; exact losses are not stated.
rows.check: Transient injected label noise improves population prediction loss relative to ordinary SGD, but tests none of the listed interventions. The noisy run remains unconverged at t = 10^6; this is not partial evidence for V4.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Diagonal linear sparse regression, α = 0.05 and α = 0.01
reader_labels.reason: SGD has better validation/test loss than GD at the same initialization, but the setting is a toy regression network rather than the version's image and language benchmarks (R1, R2). The matched effective-initialization comparison also shows GD can reach approximately the same point (R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Sparse regression trajectories and injected-label-noise variant
reader_labels.reason: The trajectory comparison reports similar SGD and SGF validation-loss behavior, and injected label noise improves the stated validation result while slowing convergence; these results qualify the comparison to training recipe and convergence status (R4, R5).
